citation: Ryter J. et al. (2025) Modeling interconnected minerals markets with multicommodity supply curves: examining the copper-cobalt-nickel system. Nature Communications. doi:10.1038/s41467-025-62570-8

dedupe_keys.name: multicommodity supply curve model of jointly produced minerals copper cobalt nickel system

description: This is an economic model of prices and production for minerals that are mined together, built at the level of individual mines so that host metals and by-products share one supply decision. It is demonstrated on the copper-cobalt-nickel system, where about 99% of cobalt is a by-product of copper or nickel mining, and calibrated by comparing simulated consumption and prices with history. It was developed by John Ryter and colleagues at the U.S. Geological Survey National Minerals Information Center with MIT, Stanford University and Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf, and published in Nature Communications on 7 August 2025. Coverage is the global market for the three metals. The article is open access under CC BY 4.0 as a US Government work, and the raw data and figure data are in the USGS ScienceBase repository; the page read does not say where the model code is. Caveats: results depend on mine cost data and on the demand shifters chosen, and the authors show that joint changes in demand give non-linear price effects, so single-commodity assumptions can mislead. For simulation it supports supply risk and capacity scenarios for metals needed by grids, batteries and renewables, for example testing how cutting cobalt supply to reduce risk could also reduce copper output. It is related to the USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries record in this catalogue, a source of production statistics for such models.
